opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. It's a great question, because I think a lot of people still build agents almost entirely through prompting. You take a strong frontier model, write a long system prompt, wire up some tools, and hope it behaves. That gets you surprisingly far, but you hit a ceiling. The agent makes the same kinds of mistakes over and over, and all you can do is add more instructions to the prompt.

What reinforcement learning changes is that the agent can actually learn from experience in the environment it's going to operate in. Instead of telling the model what to do, you let it try things: call tools, take multi-step actions, fail. Then you reward it when it gets the outcome right. Over many rollouts it picks up strategies that are hard to write down in a prompt. When to ask a clarifying question, how to recover from a tool error, when to stop searching and commit to an answer.

The way we think about it, the real differentiation isn't the RL algorithm itself. GRPO and its variants are fairly well understood now. The hard part, and where most of the value is, is in the environments and the reward signals. You need an environment that faithfully reflects the task, with realistic tools, realistic data, and realistic failure modes. And you need a verifier or reward that captures what "good" means without being trivially hackable. If your reward is sloppy, the model will find the shortcut, every time. So a lot of our work is really data and environment curation: building the tasks, checking that they're solvable but not trivial, and making sure the reward lines up with what the user actually cares about.

The other thing I'd highlight is that RL lets you get very strong results with smaller models. We've seen cases where a relatively small open model, trained with RL on a well-built environment, matches or beats much larger models on a specific agentic task. That matters a lot for companies, because it means lower cost, lower latency, and a model you can own and deploy yourself, instead of renting a general-purpose model that's only okay at your particular workflow.

So to sum it up: prompting gives you a generalist that's been told what to do. RL gives you a specialist that has practiced the job. And I think as agents move into real production settings, that practiced specialist is what people will need.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts prompt-based agents with agents that learn through reinforcement learning, and identifies that RL approach as the team’s differentiation.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the way to think about it is that most people building agents today are essentially doing prompt engineering on top of a frozen model. You take a general-purpose model, you write a very careful system prompt, you wire up some tools, maybe you add retrieval, and you hope the model generalizes to your specific task. And that works surprisingly well up to a point, but you hit a ceiling pretty quickly, because the model was never actually optimized for your environment. It was optimized to be a good general assistant.

What reinforcement learning lets you do is close that loop. Instead of just telling the model what good behavior looks like in a prompt, you let it actually interact with the environment, take actions, see the outcomes, and then you update the weights based on what worked. So the model is learning from its own experience in your specific setting, with your tools, your APIs, your failure modes. That's a fundamentally different thing from in-context learning.

And I'd say there are a few reasons this matters a lot for agents specifically. One is that agentic tasks are multi-step. It's not one prompt, one answer. You might be making twenty or thirty tool calls, and errors compound. A small mistake early on can derail the whole trajectory. Supervised fine-tuning doesn't really capture that, because you're just imitating individual steps. RL optimizes for the end outcome of the full trajectory, so the model learns things like when to verify, when to back off, when to try a different approach.

The second reason is that for a lot of these tasks, you can actually define a reward. If the agent is writing code, you can run the tests. If it's calling APIs, you can check whether the final state is correct. You don't need a human to label every step, you just need a verifiable signal at the end. And that's where RL really shines, because you can generate a lot of experience cheaply.

The third thing, which I think is underappreciated, is that RL lets you use smaller models. A model that's been RL-trained on your task can often beat a much larger general model that's just been prompted, and it's cheaper and faster at inference time. For anyone actually deploying agents in production, that's a big deal.

So to me the differentiation is really about treating the agent as something you train, not just something you configure. The environment becomes part of the training process, and that's what unlocks reliability.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts prompting a frozen model with training an agent through reinforcement learning, and calls treating the agent as something to train its differentiator.

astra-6.text:
I think the key difference is learning from the outcome of an interaction. With supervised learning, you’re essentially showing the model examples of what you want it to do. With reinforcement learning, you can give an agent a task, let it take actions, and provide feedback on whether it actually accomplished that task.

That becomes particularly interesting when success requires multiple steps. An agent might need to choose a tool, inspect the result, and change its approach. You want it to learn which decisions lead to a successful outcome, even when you can’t specify the ideal action at every step.

The challenge, of course, is defining that feedback. Can you reliably measure success? Can you give the agent an environment where it can explore and make mistakes? To me, that’s where a lot of the work is: building the conditions in which reinforcement learning produces behavior that’s actually useful.

r001.rationale: The response describes reinforcement learning as learning from interaction outcomes and contrasts it with supervised learning, but it does not identify RL as Mahesh’s team’s differentiator relative to prompting models.

sol-6.1.text:
I think reinforcement learning changes the way we think about improving an agent. You can start with a model that’s good at following instructions, give it tools, and build a workflow around it. But the real question is: does it get better at accomplishing the task through experience?

With reinforcement learning, you’re optimizing for the outcome across a sequence of decisions. The agent might need to choose a tool, interpret the result, and decide whether to try something else. An individual step can look reasonable while the overall task still fails. So you want that learning signal to reflect whether the agent actually achieved the goal.

The challenge is defining that signal. How do you measure success reliably, and how do you make sure the agent isn’t just finding a shortcut in your evaluation? That’s where the environment and the feedback become really important. For me, the opportunity is to move from agents whose behavior we manually prescribe toward agents that can learn more effective strategies from experience.

r001.rationale: The response describes reinforcement learning as a way to improve agents and contrasts learning strategies with manually prescribed behavior. It does not identify this as Mahesh’s team’s differentiator from approaches based on prompting models.
